facts.raw_span: A 67-year-old woman
31-year history of recurrent depressive disorder
depressed mood, anhedonia, nervousness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and poor sleep
beginning 5 months after COVID-19
two severe episodes responsive to escitalopram (up to 20 mg/d) and duloxetine (up to 60 mg/d)
intolerance to venlafaxine, bupropion, and trazodone
mother had mania
denied iron deficiency anemia, hypothyroidism, or substance abuse
Physical and neurologic examinations and routine laboratory tests were unremarkable
new deep itching and creeping sensations in her bilateral shoulders and arms
worse at rest, partially relieved by movement, and predominantly occurring in the evening
causing night-time sleep disturbance

concepts.why: The patient has a 31-year history of recurrent depressive disorder and is experiencing depressed mood, anhedonia, nervousness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and poor sleep.
The patient developed new deep itching and creeping sensations in her bilateral shoulders and arms after increasing duloxetine, which is a known side effect of the medication.
The patient's depressive episode began 5 months after COVID-19, suggesting a possible link between the two.
The patient has a history of recurrent depressive disorder and has not responded to multiple treatments, including escitalopram, duloxetine, venlafaxine, bupropion, and trazodone.

rationales.F02: Long history of depressive disorder increases likelihood of Major Depressive Disorder and Treatment-Resistant Depression
rationales.F04: Onset of depression after COVID-19 suggests Post-COVID-19 Depression
rationales.F05: Previous response to escitalopram and duloxetine suggests effectiveness of these treatments for Major Depressive Disorder, making Treatment-Resistant Depression less likely
rationales.F06: Intolerance to multiple antidepressants increases likelihood of Treatment-Resistant Depression
rationales.F07: Family history of mania may contribute to risk of Major Depressive Disorder
rationales.F10: New paresthesia symptoms are highly suggestive of Duloxetine-Induced Paresthesia
rationales.F11: Characteristics of paresthesia, such as worsening at rest and relief with movement, support Duloxetine-Induced Paresthesia

frontier_selector.rationale: The patient's 31-year history of recurrent depressive disorder and current symptoms of depressed mood, anhedonia, nervousness, fatigue, decreased appetite, and poor sleep strongly support Major Depressive Disorder, while the new onset of paresthesias is a separate issue that can be attributed to Duloxetine-Induced Paresthesia.
